# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding

When choosing where to hide, pick a central cell (4-6 range). This avoids being an easy extremity target while keeping your options open for future rounds. Don't rotate predictably—vary your choice based on what you've learned about your hunters' patterns.

## Shooting

When your turn to fire comes, follow the standing order unless you have strong evidence that deviating serves you better. Shooting the assigned target maintains predictability, which protects you from retaliation threats and keeps you aligned with the formal structure.

When you fire, don't mirror your hiding spot. Vary your shot location from round to round. If you hid in cell 5, fire at a different cell. This prevents your hiding pattern from being inferred from your shooting pattern.

## Claiming

When the office tells you the true result, claim it exactly. Never lie about a hit or miss. The integrity of your claims is your only credible asset in a game where all communication is public and all private information is singularly yours. A false claim destroys your reputation for the remaining rounds.

## Coalition Building

When other boats signal interest in coordination, engage with it cautiously. Acknowledge their proposals and ask for clarification on specifics rather than committing to vague unified strategies.

Do not make promises of coordinated action ("mutual defection," "protect internal group interests") unless you know you can execute them and benefit from them. These promises are binding on your reputation and may lock you into suboptimal plays later.

## Escort Claims

When filing an escort claim, only name another boat if you have evidence of mutual benefit or a specific agreement that both parties gain from the pairing. A mutual escort claim is worth 5 points each—make sure you're coordinating with someone who will reciprocate, not hoping they will.

# Playbook for hx_picket_channel

## Hide Stage
When choosing your hiding position, favor the center of the line (positions 4-6) to maximize flexibility and reduce predictability. Central positions give you defensive depth while maintaining offensive optionality.

## Note Stage
Signal your strategic alignment early. When other players establish patterns (like information gathering), explicitly join that frame rather than diverging. Use your station notes to coordinate intent clearly with allies.

## Fire Stage
Follow the standing order unless you have a specific tactical reason to deviate. The standing order provides a stable baseline; deviations should be rare and deliberate, not reactive.

When choosing your firing cell, avoid mechanical patterns like always firing at your own hide position or at the center. Vary your fire cells to reduce predictability, but keep them within the probable range where targets might hide.

## Claim Stage
Always claim truthfully what the office told you. Honesty preserves your credibility when group coordination matters. If you're caught lying about a claim, you lose leverage in all future negotiations.

## Escort Stage
Pay active attention during the entire round to track which boats are signaling coordination with you. When two boats name each other for escort, that's a mutual 10-point swing (5 to each). Don't leave these points on the table by claiming "none" without deliberation.

Maintain a mental model of who has signaled partnership with you. If you've committed to mutual coordination with another boat, honor that commitment in the escort stage by naming them back. Broken escort agreements damage future credibility more than missed shots do.

## Broader Strategy
When alignment emerges with other players around a unified strategy, commit to it explicitly and follow through. The group coordination bonus (mutual escorts) and the ability to coordinate fire against external threats (like Harbor) outweighs individual opportunism.

However: clarify what you're committing to before committing. If another player's proposal is vague, ask for specifics. Don't accept coordination framed as "we'll execute on consensus" without knowing what the consensus actually is.

Watch Harbor. It carries payoff but threatens mutiny. When Harbor signals willingness to take players off the board, treat that as a real constraint on attacking it unless you have group backing.
